ui.title: Case Files: Mohalla Detective
ui.subtitle: Stay Financially Safe
ui.rotate: Turn your phone upright to continue.
ui.intro.body: Online fraud now reaches students and families through the same apps you use every day. In this module you work as a junior analyst: each case gives you the victim's phone. You find what the attacker did, how it worked on a real person, and what would have stopped it.
ui.intro.m.inspect.body: Open the apps and tap any message, number, handle or amount you think matters.
ui.intro.m.tag.body: Name the manipulation technique at work. Not everything unusual is malicious.
ui.intro.m.rebuild.body: Place the evidence into the five stages every scam passes through.
ui.intro.m.decide.body: Choose the response that would have stopped it, then review the debrief.
ui.intro.level: How should the analyst give hints?
ui.intro.privacy: No login. Nothing leaves this device. Every name, number and amount in this module is fictional.
ui.map.heading: Case files
ui.map.mysteryBlurb: A new device, no leads. Apply the method on your own.
ui.map.masterBlurb: Compare every closed case and identify what they share.
ui.map.locked: Close the previous case to open this one.
ui.shield.protect.rule: Your OTP, PIN, password and screen are yours alone. No legitimate organisation needs you to share them.
ui.shield.verify.rule: Check every claim through a channel you find yourself: the official app, the official website, or a family member. Never use the contact details the other person gives you.
ui.shield.pause.rule: Scams depend on speed. Stop, and talk to someone you trust before you act.
ui.link.on: Linking: tap two items that may be connected
ui.hint.l3: One app on the home screen is highlighted.
ui.report.ask: Does this look like part of the attack?
ui.reason.too_good.def: A large benefit for little or no effort or qualification.
ui.reason.too_good.why: Optimism and the wish for easy gain make people skip the checks they would normally make. Genuine rewards come with conditions you can verify.
ui.reason.rushing.def: A short deadline or limited quantity that removes time to verify.
ui.reason.rushing.why: Scarcity and fear of loss push people from careful thinking to quick reaction. A genuine process survives a phone call to the real organisation.
ui.reason.pretend.def: A claim to be an official, company, friend or relative, with no proof.
ui.reason.pretend.why: People defer to apparent authority and to familiar names. Anyone can type a title or copy a logo, so a claim is not evidence.
ui.reason.secret.def: Hiding the attack from other people or from the record: keeping it secret, avoiding calls, deleting messages, blocking, disappearing.
ui.reason.secret.why: Secrecy stops the victim being challenged while it happens, and deleting or blocking removes the trail afterwards. A legitimate process never needs either.
ui.reason.grab.def: A request for an OTP, PIN, password, screen access, personal data or money.
ui.reason.grab.why: This is the objective of the attack. Everything else in the script exists to make this request feel reasonable.
ui.reason.threat.def: Threats of arrest, penalty, blocking or loss.
ui.reason.threat.why: Fear narrows attention and drives compliance. Real authorities do not threaten you over a call or video chat.
ui.reason.fine.def: This item is ordinary or safe.
analyst.correct: Correct. That goes in the evidence log.
analyst.wrongReason: Not that tactic. Look again at what this item is trying to make the person do or feel.
analyst.fineCorrect: Good judgement. An unusual item is not always an attack.
analyst.fineWrong: Look again. Something here is doing real work for the attacker.
analyst.herringAny: This one is actually safe. Part of the skill is knowing what to rule out.
analyst.context: A genuine part of the story, not an attack item.
analyst.linkOk: Same identifier across channels: one operator behind several faces.
analyst.linkFail: No shared identifier between those two. Try another pair.
analyst.allFound: All required evidence is logged. Experienced analysts still re-read the device once more.
analyst.allFoundNoGold: All evidence is logged. Close the investigation when you are ready.
analyst.goldLeft: {{n}} further item(s) are hidden in plain sight. Location not provided.
analyst.boardWrong: Reconsider what this item does within the attack.
analyst.boardIntro: Now reconstruct the attack. Place each piece of evidence in the stage where it does its work.
analyst.fixIntro: Final question: what response would have broken the attack?
analyst.fixWrong: That response would not stop it, and may make things worse. Reconsider.
analyst.fixCorrect: Correct. That is the control that works.
analyst.replayIntro: Review how the attack unfolded, stage by stage.
analyst.mystery: Unseen device. No leads. Something here is part of an attack: find it and reconstruct it.
analyst.mysteryNudge: Look for what the person is being pushed to do, and who benefits.
analyst.break: Take a break whenever you need one. Your case is saved.
analyst.finalPrompt: Explain one thing from this module to someone at home. Teaching it is how it sticks.
ui.break.body: Progress is saved on this device.
coach.1: Orientation. Each case gives you the victim's phone. Your job is to find the evidence, name the tactic, and rebuild the attack. The counter at the top tracks required evidence.
coach.2: Open Messages and tap the part of a text that looks wrong. Then choose to flag it.
coach.3: Now name the tactic. Each option has a definition: use it.
coach.4: Logged. Note that the analyst explains why the tactic works on people, not just that it is wrong. Ruling out ordinary items matters as much as finding bad ones: try the message from Appa too.
coach.6: On the board, the five stages are the structure of every scam. Today only stages 2, 3 and 4 are used.
coach.7: Last step: choose the response that would have stopped it.
ui.step.1.name: Bait
ui.step.1.def: How the target is first reached: an offer, alert or message designed to get a reaction.
ui.step.2.name: Pretext
ui.step.2.def: The false identity or story that makes the request seem legitimate.
ui.step.3.name: Pressure
ui.step.3.def: Techniques that cut time and independent checking: urgency, secrecy, threats.
ui.step.4.name: Extraction
ui.step.4.def: Where the attacker gets what they came for: a code, credentials, screen access or money.
ui.step.5.name: Exit
ui.step.5.def: How the attacker disappears and removes the trail: blocking, deleting, going unreachable.

ui.board.unused: Not used in this orientation case.

ui.help.eyebrow: If it happens to you or someone you know
ui.help.title: What to do next
ui.help.1: It is not your fault. These operations are run by professionals and fool experienced adults.
ui.help.2: Tell a trusted adult right away. Speed matters.
ui.help.3: Contact your bank or payment app using the number inside the official app, and report it.
ui.help.4: In India, the national cybercrime helpline is 1930 and reports can be filed at the national cybercrime reporting portal.
ui.master.title: What do these cases share?
ui.master.intro: Different devices, different stories. Study each stage across the cases and identify the common pattern.
ui.master.tap: Select a stage to answer its question.
ui.master.hint: Compare the cases again at this stage. What do they all do?
ui.master.reveal: The stories differ; the structure does not. Recognise the chain and you can interrupt it at any stage.
ui.master.rules: Three rules that break the chain
ui.master.q1: What do the first stages of these attacks have in common?
ui.master.q1.a: They create a strong reaction (excitement, fear or curiosity) so the target engages before thinking.
ui.master.q1.b: They always arrive through the same app.
ui.master.q1.c: They always ask for money immediately.
ui.master.q2: How do the attackers gain credibility?
ui.master.q2.a: They are genuinely the officials, friends or companies they claim to be.
ui.master.q2.b: They borrow authority or familiarity with a false identity that is hard to check in the moment.
ui.master.q2.c: They wait for the target to contact them first.
ui.master.q3: What does the pressure stage take from the target?
ui.master.q3.a: Time to think and the chance to ask someone else.
ui.master.q4: What is the attacker finally after?
ui.master.q4.a: A code, credential, screen access or money.
ui.master.q5: What does the attacker do at the end?
ui.master.q5.a: Stays in contact to help resolve the problem.
ui.master.q5.b: Disappears: blocks, deletes or becomes unreachable.
ui.rule.pause: Pause: scams depend on speed. Stop and talk to someone you trust before you act.
ui.rule.verify: Verify: check through the official app, a website you find yourself, or a family member.
ui.rule.protect: Protect: your OTP, PIN, password and screen are yours alone.
